title: Success at the Lambs Cafe and the first cover charge
summary: With Charlie Mack's reserved show party the Lambs fills up, stays open until dawn, and adds a ten-cent cover charge in May 1915.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: So Smiley wanted us to get out of town. And he said, oh, you boys ain't right. Yeah, yeah, yeah, that Charlie Mack must have been drunk. I said, I don't know, but we're going to stay, man. We got a contract for six weeks. We're going to stay. Oh, you're going to stay, huh? You're going to have a big cigar in his mind. All right. So we, I go up, I'm walking down Clark Street one day and who I run up at Charlie Mack. He said, what y'all doing? I said, man, what do we know? I said, we downstairs in the Lambs. We're dying. I said, the man's about to put the heat on this. Throw us out. I said, who, Smiley? I said, yeah. He said, you tell Smiley. And I swear there wasn't flies in the joint. Nobody would come in. He said, you tell Smiley. Make the reservation for the whole show tonight. I said, you're kidding? And there were about 75 people in the show, see? Yeah. I said, are you kidding? I know something around there. And the man told me out there before he gets ready. Tell him Charlie Mack says reserve the whole joint for 75 anyhow. And the place sat about 200. So I go down and say, Smiley says, what have you been eating oatmeal again? I said, no. I said, you know Charlie Mack, the two black crows? And so he went to verify it, and sure enough, so they went out and bought some flowers and put them all over the table. And up until 11 o'clock, there wasn't a human in the dark. We blasted in our way. Down comes these show people, and we stayed open until about 6 in the morning. Champagne full of ink water.
And they liked it in that time.

From then on, it was it. We had it made. And that was the first place that I ever know of where they put a cover charge on. Dave Barry, the guy that refereed the Dempsey fight, he was the doorman with the rope across. Because he came down the basement, see? And they put 10 cent cover charge on you. Keep the riffraff out. Now, you know that for a dime? To me, that was a funny thing, because I've been in places since. It cost you 2 and a half to get in.
Yeah, that's no cover charge. Yeah, 10 cents. 10 cents.
And so, and we stayed there. Then, uh...
What year was that? Can you remember? 1915. 1915? Yeah.
